First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{\,px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{\,px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}6{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2a}) \\  & =6\cdot (\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{2x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{2x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/61a2aafc6dadee9e392e098f77839fdd99f3bb5d30c62cf06fef1be08c4b2682.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}6{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =6\cdot (\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{2a}) \\  & =6(\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
